title: Executable Distinctions
thesis: Words become operators when they are recognized by a system authorized to act on their distinctions.
summary: A rigorous public argument about how symbols become consequential through interpreters, authority, rules, records, state transitions, and repair.

layers.label: Token
layers.question: What mark or word was presented?
layers.description: A symbol is available to be recognized. At this layer it has not yet acquired one fixed meaning or material force.

layers.label: Semantic
layers.question: What distinction did the system recognize?
layers.description: A grammar, interpreter, or institution assigns meaning, classifies the represented object, and makes some states legible.

layers.label: Operational
layers.question: What may happen because that distinction was accepted?
layers.description: Authority, rules, records, and execution paths permit or prohibit actions that change reachable state and distribute consequence.

safeguards: Words do not possess power in isolation; consequential force comes from systems authorized and equipped to act.
A person is not exhausted by the software or institutional representation applied to them.
Vocabulary overlap and useful analogy do not establish formal equivalence or operational homology.
claimCeiling: A conceptual public argument supported by software and institutional examples. It does not establish that every word is executable, that human institutions are reducible to computers, or that cross-domain correspondences are formally equivalent.
